title: Teaching by example
hookLine: the first teaching is how you live
tomorrow: why did the Buddha almost keep it to himself?

cards: Little kids copy everything: the way you fold your hands, the way you sigh at your phone. At the chùa on Sunday, the smallest ones will copy Mai before they understand a word she says.
An old story starts the same way, on a city street. A wandering seeker named Sariputta is walking through Rajagaha when he sees a monk on his alms round. The monk isn't preaching.
He's just walking: eyes lowered, steps unhurried, robe neat, bowl held quietly. Sariputta can't stop watching. Whoever taught this man to move like that, he thinks, is someone worth finding.

teach.b: The monk is Assaji, one of the Buddha's first companions, and the Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells what happens next.

Sariputta waits until the alms round is done, then asks him: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji's answer is humble. He says he's new to this and can't explain the teaching at length, only its gist.
Then he gives one short line about causes: whatever arises from a cause, the Buddha has shown its cause, and how it ends. That's enough. Sariputta's life turns on it.
The walk came first. Before a single word, a stranger's way of moving had already said: there's something here worth asking about.
That's why Buddhists put sila, conduct, at the base of the path, and why monks train in small things, like how to walk, eat and wear the robe. The training is the teaching, made visible.
The Dhammapada says it plainly, in Max Müller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others."
For Mai, that's good news. She doesn't need to know everything by Sunday. The kids will learn first from how she sits, how she talks to the shy one, and whether her phone stays in her bag.

how: Buddhist monks and nuns train in small points of conduct (how to walk, eat and wear the robe) as part of the path; at temple classes, lay teachers often teach children first by how they sit and speak.

o: copying a teacher until you can teach too
teaching only through stories with a moral
teaching others through the way you live

games.q: who did what on that street — tap the pairs.
p: walked his alms round, calm and quiet
conduct, at the base of the path

s: Assaji won Sariputta over with a long sermon
he gave one short line about causes. his walk had already done the work.
your example only teaches once you know a lot
Assaji called himself new and gave only the gist; Sariputta was moved by how he moved.
monks train in how to walk, eat and wear the robe
small conduct is part of the training: the teaching made visible.

games.q: your little cousin begs to try your meditation app, then watches you scroll on it for an hour. by today's story, what teaches her most?
o: what she sees you actually do with it.
the best guided meditation in the app.
a clear explanation of what meditation is.
games.why: Sariputta was won before Assaji said a word. kids read the walk before the talk.

practice: For the sit, take the posture you'd be glad for a child to copy: feet on the floor, back easy, hands resting, face soft. Nobody's watching, so hold it kindly anyway, the way Assaji walked when he thought no one was looking.
When your shoulders creep up, let them settle again.

wordCard.voice: Teaching by example: the lesson people take from how you live, before you've said a thing. Assaji's walk taught first.

orig.note: Pali: conduct, virtue. Buddhists put it at the base of the path; it's where teaching by example lives.

carryVoice: Keep this one: by example, the way Assaji's walk spoke before his words did. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.23 (Sariputta meets Assaji in Rajagaha)

sources.q: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others.
